content: 1. The International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision (ICD-10), published in 2004, provides a standardized framework for categorizing health-related problems. 2. General comments and recommendations from treaty monitoring bodies aim to interpret the content and application of human rights conventions. These comments clarify the reporting obligations of State Parties concerning specific provisions and suggest methods for implementing treaty provisions. 3. Health is defined as a state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease or infirmity. 4. A health system encompasses all organizations, individuals, and actions primarily intended to promote, restore, or maintain health. 5. Health workers include all individuals engaged in activities aimed at improving health. While this can include unpaid caregivers such as parents caring for sick children or individuals practicing self-care, available data on health workers typically focus on those involved in paid activities. 6. Human rights standards refer to the meaning and scope of human rights as outlined in international treaties and interpreted by human rights bodies, including international, regional, and national courts, as well as human rights committees. 7. Incomplete abortion is characterized by the clinical presence of an open cervical os and bleeding, where not all products of conception have been expelled from the uterus, or the expelled products are inconsistent with the estimated duration of pregnancy. Common symptoms include vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain. 8. An international human rights treaty, also known as a covenant or convention, is a legal instrument adopted by the international community of States, typically through the United Nations General Assembly. These treaties outline human rights and corresponding obligations that are legally binding on ratifying States. 9. Intrauterine fetal demise (IUFD) refers to the death of a fetus at any point during pregnancy. 10. A mandatory waiting period is a legally or policy-imposed requirement to wait a specified amount of time between requesting and receiving abortion care. 11. Medical methods of abortion involve the use of pharmacological agents to terminate a pregnancy. 12. Mental health is a state of well-being in which individuals realize their potential, cope with normal life stresses, work productively, and contribute to their community. 13. Miscarriage, or spontaneous abortion, is the loss of a pregnancy before 24 weeks of gestation, prior to fetal viability outside the uterus. Clinical signs include vaginal bleeding, often accompanied by abdominal pain and cramping. If the pregnancy has been expelled, the miscarriage is classified as complete or incomplete based on whether uterine tissues remain. 14. Missed abortion refers to the cessation of pregnancy development, where embryonic or fetal tissue, or an empty gestational sac, remains in the uterus with a closed cervical os. Symptoms may include pain and/or bleeding, or there may be no symptoms at all. 15. Osmotic dilators are short, thin rods made of seaweed (laminaria) or synthetic material. When placed in the cervical os, they absorb moisture and expand, gradually dilating the cervix. 16. Policy refers to laws, regulations, procedures, administrative actions, incentives, or voluntary practices implemented by governments and other institutions. 17. Post-abortion care involves providing services after an abortion, such as contraceptive services, management of complications, and linkage to other necessary services within the community or beyond. 18. Primary health care (PHC) is a whole-of-society approach to health that aims to achieve the highest possible level of health and well-being through equitable distribution. It focuses on addressing people's needs and preferences early along the continuum of care, from health promotion and disease prevention to treatment, rehabilitation, and palliative care, as close as possible to their everyday environment. 19. Quality of care (QoC) in health care encompasses six dimensions: effectiveness, efficiency, accessibility, acceptability/person-centeredness, equity, and safety. Effective care adheres to evidence-based practices and improves health outcomes. Efficient care optimizes resource use and minimizes waste. Accessible care is timely, geographically reachable, and provided in settings appropriate to medical needs. Acceptable care respects individual preferences and cultural contexts. Equitable care ensures consistent quality regardless of personal characteristics. Safe care minimizes risks and harm to service users. 20. Self-care refers to the ability of individuals, families, and communities to promote health, prevent disease, maintain health, and manage illness and disability with or without the support of a health worker. It includes health promotion, disease prevention, self-medication, caregiving for dependents, seeking professional care when necessary, and rehabilitation, including palliative care. 21. Self-management of abortion involves individuals managing the entire process of medical abortion or specific steps, such as assessing eligibility, self-administering medications without direct supervision, and evaluating the success of the abortion process. 22. Social enterprise, or social business, is a business model with specific social objectives as its primary purpose. These enterprises aim to maximize societal and environmental benefits while generating profits, which are primarily used to fund social programs. 23. Social franchising is a system of contractual relationships, often run by non-governmental organizations, that uses the structure of commercial franchising to achieve social goals. Unlike commercial franchising, which is profit-driven, social franchising focuses on delivering social benefits. 24. Social marketing applies marketing techniques to address social problems. It aims to persuade or motivate individuals to adopt behaviors or actions that are widely recognized as beneficial. While it cannot create behavior, it facilitates acceptance and willingness to adopt the behavior, with a predominantly preventive strategy. 25. Surgical methods of abortion involve transcervical procedures to terminate pregnancy, such as vacuum aspiration and dilation and evacuation (D&E). 26. Telemedicine, or telehealth, is a mode of health service delivery where providers and clients, or providers and consultants, are separated by distance. This can involve communication via telephone, video link, email, or text/audio messages, and may include remote consultations or the transmission of medical data (e.g., images, notes, videos) from clients to health workers. 27. Third-party authorization refers to a legal or policy requirement for a party other than the pregnant individual (e.g., parent, guardian, spouse, partner, health worker, health authority, or judicial authority) to authorize an abortion, even when all other legal requirements for lawful abortion are met. 28. Treaty monitoring bodies are committees of independent experts designated to monitor compliance with international human rights treaties. Their primary function is to assess State compliance through the examination of State reports. 29. Universal health coverage (UHC) ensures that all individuals have access to necessary health services, including promotive, preventive, curative, rehabilitative, and palliative care, of sufficient quality to be effective, without exposing users to financial hardship. 30. Vacuum aspiration, whether electrical (EVA) or manual (MVA), involves evacuating the contents of the uterus using a plastic or metal cannula attached to a vacuum source. EVA uses an electric vacuum pump, while MVA employs a hand-held, hand-activated aspirator. This method is effective up to 15–16 weeks of pregnancy or for post-abortion care cases requiring larger cannulae for effective vacuuming.
